intro: Every animal built from your sheets KM-P4 and KM-P8, reviewed by the strict rules (docs/ASSET_REVIEW.md): each one from all eight sides, each of its motions animated at 24 frames and at the game's own speed, its source and its parts beside it, and seventeen checks with their results.

Every motion is now the game's own code for that animal (WallCat, Dog, GroundBird, TreeSquirrel, PondDuck, CritterIdle, FlitButterfly), and every part that bends in the real animal bends in the model. The same code drives the game, so what you see here is what plays.
fixed: Knees where the animal's are (your latest clips). Each leg had one joint, halfway down: a dog's or a cat's front leg bent in the middle of its forearm, and a hind leg above its hock. Now a front leg bends at the elbow under the belly and folds back at the wrist low down, as a dog's and a cat's do in each step; a hind leg bends at the hock; and every joint bends the way the animal's does, never the way the photo's pose suggested. The Shiba's far hind leg, only a pale strip in its photo, is now a copy of the near one, and the pale wedge it left under the belly is gone. The block at the cat's elbow and the sparrow's pale lump are gone. A sparrow's hop now crouches, springs with its feet trailing, tucks them up under it and lands; a pigeon shuffles with low steps.

One body that bends (learning D21). Each animal was a set of rigid photo pieces turning over its body, and every joint showed their edges: flaps at the tops of the legs, a straight cut under the chest, blocks below the neck. Each animal is now one skin on a skeleton, bending at its shoulders, hips, knees, ankles, neck and tail, so nothing shows an edge. The far legs are a second skin behind the body, without the patch of flank or breast that used to swing out with them.

Real feet. A bird's foot was the photo's side view of its toes, a flat plate that looked big and glued down from every other angle. Each bird now stands on three toes forward and one back, built in the round. Every foot lifts heel first and rolls over its toes at the end of a step; in the swing a bird curls its toes and a cat or dog folds its paw; it lands flat.

Movements of the real animal. A four-legged animal's back tilts gently with its stride, its head held steady. A bird's neck bends to peck. Pigeons, doves and the wagtail hold their heads still in the air and thrust them forward with each step, herons and egrets less, crows and gulls a little. Perched birds look about in quick turns and holds. The egret's plumes hang as it pecks. The koi's head answers its tail and its front fins scull. The dragonfly's hind wings beat ahead of its forewings. An insect's antennae and abdomen stay still.

Wings that beat like wings (your second set of clips). The sparrow's, swallow's and white-eye's wings went up and down stiff, the same shape both ways, like paddles. A real wing beats down spread and a little forward, then folds at the wrist and sweeps back on the way up, and the body lifts with each downstroke. Every small flyer now beats that way, each with its own stroke: the sparrow and white-eye fold deepest, the swallow beats shallow and sweeps back the most, the dove beats widest. Wings and tails are now thin, as they are, not rounded into a ridge and a lump, and the tail tilts with each beat. The bulbul's tail, which fans out wider than its body, was a faceted block; it is now a flat fan too.

A squirrel that bounds. The running squirrel slid along on still legs while its body rocked. It now has legs and a back that bend: the hind feet land ahead of the front ones, push off together and stretch out behind, the back gathers at each landing and stretches in the air, and the tail streams behind. The game's squirrel bounds the same way in a dash, hops smaller when it forages, and scampers up a trunk. Looked at in large frames, its first bound still had the flaps you saw on other animals: grey shards of ground at its front paws (the photo's shadow, taken in with the paws) and dark flaps under its belly (its far legs reach under the belly in the photo, so their thighs were a patch of belly that swung out). The ground is now left out, and the near legs' copies stand in for the far ones.

Each leg is one leg (learning D20). I looked at every frame at full size and at each model's parts in colour. Thirteen models were cut wrongly, though every check had passed. Five birds and the Shiba walked on four legs: two legs that touch in the picture were found as one, then copied. The pecking pigeon and the dove walked a toe under legs left in the body, and the hopping crow and sparrow kept their raised leg in the body as a third. Each bird's legs are now drawn on its sheet, near and far. A far leg is copied from the near one only where the picture hides it (the standing crow, the wagtail, the Shiba's far front leg), and a leg raised mid-step is taken out.

Feet stay flat, birds bend at the heel. Toes were rigid in the shin and dipped into the floor whenever the leg turned, by up to a fifth of a bird's height. Check 16 measured only one point per foot. Every foot is now a part of its own, turning at the ankle and kept level, and check 16 measures every leg. A bird's bare leg is one bone hinged at the heel, as a real bird's is (cut at its middle, it had a knee no bird has). Its thigh is a feathered drumstick inside the body, so the leg never parts from the belly.

Tails and heads hold only themselves. Tails drawn as boxes took a strip of rump or haunch with them (the sitting cat, tanuki, Shiba and tuxedo) or cut the tail in two (the lying tuxedo). The tanuki's tail took half its far hind leg, and the calico's missed its lower stripes. Heads drawn as boxes took wing or breast as the birds looked about. Each is now drawn round its tail or head and neck. A spike that stood up at the back of the neck whenever a bird pecked (the pigeon and the dove since the first review) is gone: it was a strip of body left beside the head.

Fins, plumes, a tail and a wingbeat. The koi's front fins stay whole with the body instead of half-swinging with the tail. The heron's and egret's plumes turn with their heads. The Shiba's curled tail sways side to side over its back, as a Shiba's does, instead of swinging up and down and opening a slit under it. The dragonfly beats its wings about flat instead of clapping them like a butterfly. The ginger cat's chin lost a grey block of backdrop, and the crows' scaly toes are whole again.
New: check 17 and a part map. Beside every source is the model's parts in colour at full size, and check 17 says what was looked at on it.

Walks rebuilt from your recordings. Legs were one rigid piece swung from the hip. Every walking leg is now jointed (thigh, shin, foot), each foot planted while the body passes over it, then lifted and carried forward. Cats, the tanuki and the Shiba walk in four beats and run at a trot; the walking cats also tuck their legs through WallCat's bound (learning D19).
Birds walk instead of bouncing. Birds step on jointed legs, their heads nodding; sparrows hop with both feet; a peck tips the body on planted feet, only as far as the legs can keep them planted.

Tails and wings bend. Every tail is three links and every bird's wing two, each link trailing the one before, so a swish or a wingbeat runs down it like a whip. The koi sweep their tails as they swim, the turtle paddles its flippers, the wagtail pumps its tail. Insects keep rigid wings, as real ones are.

Every motion is the game's. The sitting cats swish as WallCat swishes (no more head turning the game never does), the Shiba wags as the Dog wags, the squirrels flick and dash as TreeSquirrel does, the perched birds look about as CritterIdle moves them, the koi and turtle swim as PondDuck moves them. The numbers are in the kit's manifest for the level builder.
Feet are measured. Check 16 reads every foot's height through every motion: none goes below the ground, a walk always has a foot down, a peck moves no foot.
Earlier in this review: legs that came off (D16), tips that vanished from behind (D17), cut-outs that lost fur and feathers (D18), the heron's missing lower legs, the insects' wings and the swim.
limits: Top, bottom, front and back of an animal built from its side come from that side picture alone: the belly and back are the side's fur stretched and mirrored. The game shows the right side.
The seven in flight are built from one view: from the side each is a thin plate. They are a few pixels across on the phone; check 4 marks each as a known limit.
Still on purpose: the calico asleep, the basking turtle, the swallow on its wire and the drying cormorant have no part their behaviour moves; they stay still, as in the game.
Too quick for a GIF: a wingbeat and a butterfly's flutter are slowed and say so on the frame (x1/2, x1/4); everything else plays at its real speed.

A far leg copied from the near one where the picture can't give it whole: the standing crow's and the wagtail's far tarsus, the Shiba's far front leg (only a paw shows), the hopping crow's and sparrow's raised leg (a raised leg can't plant), and the running squirrel's far legs (in the photo they reach under its belly mid-stride, and swung out as flaps in a bound). Check 17 names each copy.
pending: Four-view pictures of the walkers (KAMAKURA_BUILD Step 4c, BASE KM-S2): each walking animal and ground bird built from one photo of it mid-stride keeps that photo's limits (copied far legs, joints placed by anatomy rather than seen, the width and face guessed). Sheets of each standing square, all legs whole and apart, from the side, above, front and back, let every leg be cut at the joints the picture shows.
The large birds in flight (black kite, gull, crow, pigeon, heron, egret, cormorant) wait for their four-view KM-S1 sheets (KAMAKURA_BUILD Step 4b). The perched and standing ones are here.
The frog, snail, crab and starfish sit on photo backgrounds on the sheets and need their own cut-outs.
In the game: nothing is placed in a level yet; the kit's FBX files are built, and the reference-phone check comes with the first level that uses them.
